name: Photography is an Art of Observation: Learn to see
description: Photography is an art of observation. Learn to notice light, gestures and relationships, then use framing, timing and technique to express what matters.

step.name: Make curiosity a practical habit
step.text: On your next walk, use the ten-minute observation exercise at one stopping point. You can return to the same place on another day and notice how weather, light and activity change its possibilities. Stay long enough to explore what interests you, and remain ready to respond. For a related perspective on patience and responding to conditions, read The Way of Wu Wei .

step.name: Look beyond the subject that first attracted you
step.text: When a subject holds your attention, it is easy to overlook its surroundings. A bright sign, an overlapping branch or a person at the edge may become much more noticeable when you look at the finished photograph. Practise shifting your attention between the subject and the rest of the scene. Once you have chosen your frame, check whether those surrounding details support what you want to show.

step.name: Use experience to anticipate
step.text: Familiarity with a subject gives you clues about what might happen next. Watching a person repeat an action, waves reach the shore or light move across a landscape can help you choose your position and prepare the camera. Keep watching as events unfold. If the action or light changes in an unexpected way, adjust your response rather than holding on to the photograph you originally imagined.

step.name: Review one decision at a time
step.text: After a session, choose a photograph and recall what made you take it. Can you see that reason clearly in the image? Identify one choice about timing, viewpoint or framing that helped, and one you would change. This gives your next practice session a useful focus. For a fuller review method, continue to Lesson 34: How to Improve Your Photography Composition .

step.name: Connect observation with a choice
step.text: You notice a lone figure in an open landscape. If the sense of scale interests you, include enough of the surroundings to show how small the person appears. You notice a brief exchange between two people. Watch their gestures and the space between them. Choose a moment and viewpoint that make their relationship visible. You notice the rhythm of branches in soft light. Explore where the shapes overlap and separate. Choose a frame that makes the pattern clear while preserving the atmosphere that attracted you.

step.name: Use technique to support your intention
step.text: Choose depth of field according to how much context matters. Choose shutter speed according to how you want movement to appear. Adjust your viewpoint to organise the relationships you have noticed. The composition tools in Lesson 26 can help you make these decisions. Start with your reason for taking the photograph, then choose the tools that help express it.
